messages.subject: Re: Calculating back feed requirements based on pA
messages.subject_clean: Calculating back feed requirements based on pA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Yes of course. Please find below an example code. In the code, we use Atlantic salmon as species and simulate the growth up to harvest size (5500g).
>From this code, 1.5-1.9kg dry feed is needed to grow a 5.5kg fish (wetmass) depending on the method used to estimate the ingested feed.

As a point of comparison, in fish farming we generally observe that 1 to 1.2 kg of dry feed is needed per kg of fish (wetmass) produced. This means that we generally use 5.5 to 6.6kg feed to grow a 5.5 kg fish. So the estimates we obtain are indeed way lower than what is observed in fish farms. In salmon fish farms, the feed is also monitored through cameras and sensors, meaning that there is very limited uneaten feed in these systems.

Let me know if you have any ideas to explain these results.

FYI, the dry matter content of a salmon is about 30% which means that a 5.5 kg fish equals 1.65 kg dry mass fish.

getwd()
setwd("C:/Users/chary/Desktop")
#rm

library(data.table)
library(NicheMapR)
library(R.matlab)

# this packages has a function for producing formatted tables.

allStat<-readMat('allStat.mat') # this will take a few minutes
save(allStat, file = 'allstat.Rda') # save it as an R data file for faster future loading

load('allStat.Rda')
species <- "Salmo.salar"

species.name <http://species.name> <- gsub(pattern = "[.]", " ", species)
ndays <- 365*3 # number days to run the simulation for
div <- 1 # time step divider (1 = days, 24 = hours, etc.) - keep small if using Euler method

Tbs <- rep(20, ndays * div) # °C, body temperature
starvetime <- 0 # length of low food period when simulating starvation
X <- 100 # J/cm2 base food density
Xs <- c(rep(X, ndays * div / 2), rep(0.000005, starvetime), rep(X, ndays * div / 2 - starvetime + 1)) # food density (J/cm2 or J/cm3)
E_sm <- 350 # J/cm3, volume-specific stomach energy
clutchsize <- 100000 # -, clutch size

mass.unit <- 'g'
length.unit <- 'mm'
Euler <- 1 # use Euler integration (faster but less accurate) (1) or deSolve's ODE solve (0)
plot <- 1 # plot results?
start.stage <- 1 # stage in life cycle to start (0 = egg, 1 = juvenile, 2 = puberty)

deb_dep_i<- rundeb(species = species, ndays = ndays, div = div, Tbs = Tbs, clutchsize = clutchsize, Xs = Xs, mass.unit = mass.unit, length.unit = length.unit, start.stage = start.stage, E_sm = E_sm, Euler = Euler, plot = plot)
deb_dep_i <- as.data.table(deb_dep_i$debout)

#only select weight until harvest
deb_dep_i_hw<-deb_dep_i[wetmass<5500]

#feed
energy_feed<-21038.67 #j/g DE in the feed

#feed eaten estimated
#by DEB
GDRYFOOD_sum<-deb_dep_i_hw[,sum(GDRYFOOD)]

#calculate gram of feed eaten by the energy content of the feed and the p_A
gram_feed<-deb_dep_i_hw[,sum(p_A)]/energy_feed

messages.subject: missing data from 'runauto' function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!
I am currently trying to estimate microclimate information using the microclima function 'runauto' using microclima+NicheMapR. The function runs, but the output lacks temperatures for ~76 consecutive days of the year largely corresponding to the summer. Do you think there is a straightforward way of solving this? The same days of data are missing for every year I've attempted to model microclimate. I've included the code below, and for context, this is in western North Carolina, USA.

elev <- get_dem(r=NA, resolution=150, lat=35.594503, long=-81.710965, xdims=550, ydims=300)
range <- runauto(r=elev, dstart="01/01/2011", dfinish="02/01/2012", hgt=0.01, l=NA, x=NA, habitat=4, r.is.dem=TRUE, cad.effects=TRUE, coastal=FALSE, plot.progress=FALSE)

Best,
Tom

messages.subject: Re: Calculating back feed requirements based on pA
messages.subject_clean: Calculating back feed requirements based on pA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Killian,

I see what you mean. One possibility is the digestive efficiency kappa_X is less than the default assumption of 0.8 (but that would need to approach about 0.25). Another is that the parameters estimated are not appropriate and imply a higher growth efficiency kappa_G <- (d_V * mu_V) / (w_V * E_G). Marko Jusup might have some insights here from his experience modelling tuna.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Thanks for your ideas.
Regarding digestive efficiency, based on calculation and experimental studies, 80% would be a correct estimate. This value necessarily depends on the type of feed, but the range is about 80-95% for feeds used in Salmon aquaculture. By the way, a previous DEB publication on Salmon by Fore et al. (2016) used 75% for digestive efficiency.

That is possible that the parameters (including the growth effiency parameter) are not appropriate, but then I'm wondering why growth simulations are close enough to in situ observations .

Is it possible to have one variable (like growth) correctly estimated while others (like feed intake) show some discrepancies?

Killian

PS: I'll try to contact Marko Jusup. Thanks.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Killian,

I did ask Marko about it and he said:

"Killian is right about kap_X being around 0.8 for fish, especially in aquaculture. Also, for salmon fed with dry feed, conversion ratios of 1 kg (wet) of salmon per 1 kg of feed is about right, although even values somewhat below 1 are possible (about 0.9 but probably not less than that). As for the mismatch that they are getting by running the code with parameters from AmP, I can’t say that’s very surprising. The values in the database should not be used for any sort of “precision” modeling, without first checking them against a wide array of datasets on ontogeny of the species of interest".

One possible reason would be, for instance, that the food composition is not well matched to the fish's body composition, which gets into the stochiometric parameters of the DEB theory and possibly the need for more than one reserve to account for this. Another is that the gut microbiome is taking a chunk of the energy. I asked chatGPT how much this could be for fish and it said up to 30% but I don't know if it was just making stuff up :). It will be interesting to get to the bottom of it though as the DEB theory is being very explicit about the mass transformations and is based on generalised, realistic biological chemical transformation processes. So the calculation should be physically and chemically consistent but there might be some interesting biological reason for the discrepancy you see.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anouch,

Sorry to take a while with this - it does seem that the integrator is having trouble with the sudden jumps in rainfall. I've just pushed a change to micro_ncep and micro_era5 so that when you pass hourly rainfall to the model but set rainhourly=0, it will aggregate the hourly rainfall to daily and make it fall at midnight. Can you give this new version a try in this way and see if it works? I haven't had a chance to test it myself.

All the best,
Mike

For example, on GPS coordinates (-114.6668, 50.63571), it models the right snow depth over the entire period, but on coordinates (-114.6661, 50.63590) it stops modelling after the 30 April 2019 (any variable).

> > > > > > > > Also when I made this change initially, I forgot about some subsequent code that caused a rather big problem (hourly rain vector became one value, zero!). I fixed that problem this morning so I think it's all working properly now.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Monday, July 25, 2022 at 5:24:04 PM UTC+10 NicheMapR wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi everyone,
> > > > > > > > > I wanted to alert you to a change I've made to micro_era5 and micro_ncep to prevent them from getting stuck in endless loops in some circumstances. The short story is it won't make any difference to your calculations other than preventing the endless loops.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The longer story is that I found that in some places the integrator was having difficulty finding a solution on days with a relatively large daily precipitation. In the microclimate model, the precipitation meant to fall daily at midnight. However, because the input data for micro_ncep and micro_era5 can start at times other than midnight, depending on the timezone (because it is based on UTC), there were situations where the precipitation was falling when there was high solar radiation. I've fixed it by putting the daily rainfall into the hourly rainfall input vector, on the hours that are local solar midnight.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hope that makes sense. The change is presently only on the github version.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > All the best,
> > > > > > > > > Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using the endoR function in NicheMapR to predict the cutaneous evaporative water loss of the African elephant. However, the predited value was much smaller than reported. I suspect that maybe elephant's scuptured skin matters in this gap. I wonder which parameter can be adjusted to make up for it or if there are any other factors matter.

Any advice would be most appreciated!

Best regards
Yize Liu
